latin: Quīntilī Vāre, legiōnēs redde!
translation: Quintilius Varus, give me back my legions!
context: After three legions were wiped out in the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9, Augustus is said to have beaten his head on doors for months, shouting this at the dead general.
attribution_note: Text verified in Suetonius (Latin Library spells Quintili; some editions Quinctili). Suetonius writes "ferunt" (they say), a reported anecdote.

teaching_value.note: Vocative of an -ius name (Quīntilī) and a -us name (Vāre), an imperative, and a 3rd-decl. accusative plural.

image.alt: Stand-in image: a Roman soldier's tombstone from Britain (Rufus Sita, Thracian auxiliary cavalryman, Gloucester), not one of Varus's legionaries
image.credit: Wikimedia Commons · Unknown authorUnknown author

latin: Hominēs, dum docent, discunt.
translation: People learn while they teach.
context: Seneca tells his friend Lucilius to keep company with people who make him better, because teaching and learning run both ways.

teaching_value.note: Four words, two 3rd-conj. present 3rd-pl. verbs (docent/discunt) and the dum "while" clause. Usable as early as Unit 3.

image.alt: Roman marble portrait bust of a boy
image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access)

latin: Omnia, Lūcīlī, aliēna sunt, tempus tantum nostrum est.
translation: Everything, Lucilius, belongs to others; only time is ours.
context: From the opening letter of Seneca's Moral Letters: nature gave us one possession, time, and we let others take it from us.

teaching_value.note: sum with predicate adjectives in sing. and plural (sunt/est), vocative Lūcīlī, possessive noster. All core words.

image.alt: "Pseudo-Seneca" head, British Museum (identity uncertain)
image.credit: British Museum · Unknown artistUnknown artist

latin: Sunt bona, sunt quaedam mediocria, sunt mala plūra quae legis hīc.
translation: Some things you read here are good, some are average, more are bad.
context: Martial teases his friend Avitus, admitting that his own book of epigrams is a mixed bag. That, he says, is simply how a book gets made.

teaching_value.note: sunt + neuter plural adjectives used as nouns (bona, mala); plūra as a comparative; a simple relative clause. A good pattern for a lot of drills.

image.alt: Roman wax writing tablet
image.credit: Wikimedia Commons (CC0) · Mx. Granger

latin: Hīc sumus fēlīcēs; valeāmus rēctē.
translation: Here we are happy; may we fare well.
context: Someone scratched this near Pompeii's amphitheatre, perhaps on a good day at the games. Ordinary Romans wrote cheerful notes like this all over their walls.

source.work: Graffito, Pompeii, Campus by the amphitheatre (II.7.1)

attribution_note: AGP text: "Ic (:hic) sumus felices valiamus (:valeamus) recte". Spelling is normalized here. AGP lists CIL IV 1321 and 8657.

teaching_value.note: sumus + a predicate nominative plural (fēlīcēs). The subjunctive valeāmus is a glossed preview.

image.alt: Pompeian fresco of the amphitheatre riot of AD 59
image.credit: Naples Archaeological Museum · U.D.F., Paris

latin: Salūs populī suprēma lēx estō.
translation: Let the welfare of the people be the highest law.
context: Part of the law code Cicero drafted, in an old-fashioned style, for an ideal Roman state. This clause sets out the duty of the consuls.
attribution_note: Later a political motto (John Locke, Second Treatise §158); Cicero's text has "Ollīs salūs populī suprēma lēx estō" ("For them [the consuls]...").

teaching_value.note: Five words: genitive populī, adjective agreement (suprēma lēx), legal future imperative estō. A model sentence for the genitive.

image.alt: Bust of Cicero, Palazzo Nuovo, Rome
image.credit: “Bust of Cicero (1st-cent. BC) - Palazzo Nuovo - Musei Capitolini - Rome 2016” by José Luiz, CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0), via Wikimedia Commons; modified: background removed (cut-out), cropped, resized

latin: Ubi sōlitūdinem faciunt, pācem appellant.
translation: Where they make a desert, they call it peace.
context: Tacitus puts these words in the mouth of Calgacus, a Caledonian chief, as he condemns Roman conquest before the battle of Mons Graupius in AD 83.
attribution_note: Text verified; the speech is composed by Tacitus, and whether Calgacus said anything like it is unknowable. The text begins atque ubi…; most editions number it 30.5 (some 30.4).

teaching_value.note: Two clean S-V-O clauses: accusative + 3rd-pl. present verbs. Teaches the ubi clause. An unforgettable look at Rome from the other side.

image.alt: Stand-in image: Gallic warrior statue, Musée de la Romanité, Nîmes (not a Caledonian)
image.credit: “Musee-romanite-guerrier-casque-1” by Christelle Molinié, CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0), via Wikimedia Commons; modified: background removed (cut-out), cropped, resized

latin: M·AGRIPPA·L·F·COS·TERTIVM·FECIT — Mārcus Agrippa, Lūcī fīlius, cōnsul tertium, fēcit.
translation: Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, consul for the third time, made (this).
context: Hadrian rebuilt the Pantheon about AD 125 but kept Agrippa's original dedication. Visitors still read it over the portico today.

source.date: 27-25 BC text; rebuilt under Hadrian c. AD 125

attribution_note: Text per Wikipedia "Pantheon, Rome" (citing CIL VI 896); verify against EDR/EDCS before shipping.

teaching_value.note: A real stone sentence: nominative subject plus verb. Teaches Roman abbreviations (M., L. F., COS). The expanded form uses core words.

image.alt: 19th-c. photograph of the Pantheon portico with the Agrippa inscription
image.credit: Hallwyl Museum, Stockholm · Unknown authorUnknown author

latin: CAVE CANEM — Cavē canem!
translation: Beware of the dog!
context: At the entrance of a Pompeian house, a chained black dog in mosaic warns visitors. Buried by Vesuvius in AD 79, it still greets tourists today.
person: House of the Tragic Poet, Pompeii

source.work: Floor mosaic inscription, House of the Tragic Poet, Pompeii

teaching_value.note: Accusative object canem with the 2nd-conj. imperative cavē (preview). Two words, everyday Latin.

image.alt: "Cave canem" dog mosaic, House of the Tragic Poet, Pompeii
image.credit: “Cave Canem Poeta Trágico 03” by Miguel Hermoso Cuesta, CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0), via Wikimedia Commons; modified: cropped to 3:4, resized

latin: Rōmula hīc cum Staphylō morātur.
translation: Romula hangs out here with Staphylus.
context: A bit of Pompeian gossip about a couple, scratched on a wall. It shows ordinary people, not emperors, and the gossip they wrote on their walls.

teaching_value.note: Nominative subject + verb; cum + ablative and the deponent morātur are glossed previews. Short and human.

image.alt: Via dell'Abbondanza, Pompeii
image.credit: “Pompeii Via dell' Abbondanza 01” by Ad Meskens, CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0), via Wikimedia Commons; modified: cropped to 3:4, resized

latin: Nōn amō tē, Sabidī, nec possum dīcere quārē: hoc tantum possum dīcere, nōn amō tē.
translation: I don't like you, Sabidius, and I can't say why: I can only say this: I don't like you.
context: A two-line epigram of pure dislike. In 1680 Tom Brown famously adapted it into English as "I do not love thee, Doctor Fell."

teaching_value.note: amō + accusative tē, vocative Sabidī. possum + infinitive is a glossed preview. The repeated frame makes it easy to remember.

image.alt: Engraving of Martial after an ancient gem (identification traditional)
image.credit: Wikimedia Commons · Unknown

learn_more.label: I do not love thee, Doctor Fell

latin: Homō sum: hūmānī nīl ā mē aliēnum putō.
translation: I am human: I consider nothing human foreign to me.
context: A nosy neighbour, Chremes, defends asking about another man's troubles. His excuse became one of the most quoted lines of Roman humanism.

teaching_value.note: Homō sum, then 1st-conj. putō with an object and predicate. The genitive hūmānī and ā mē are glossed previews.

image.alt: Illustrated Terence manuscript (Vat. lat. 3868), Andria 1.1
image.credit: Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana · unknown Carolingian scribe, 9th century AD

learn_more.label: Homo sum, humani nihil a me alienum puto

latin: Hōrum omnium fortissimī sunt Belgae.
translation: Of all these, the bravest are the Belgae.
context: Caesar explains why the Belgae were the toughest Gauls: they lived farthest from Roman luxuries and closest to the warlike Germans.

teaching_value.note: sunt + nominative plural subject and predicate. The genitive and the superlative are glossed previews. A companion to "Gallia est omnis dīvīsa".

image.alt: Green-stone portrait of Julius Caesar, Berlin
image.credit: “Portrait bust of Julius Caesar (Berlin Ant Sk 342) 02” by Mark Landon, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0), via Wikimedia Commons; modified: background removed (cut-out), cropped, resized

latin: Est modus in rēbus, sunt certī dēnique fīnēs.
translation: There is a measure in things; there are, in short, fixed limits.
context: Horace mocks greed. Between the miser and the spendthrift, he says, there is a sensible middle, the root of his ideal of moderation.

teaching_value.note: est/sunt as "there is/are", in + ablative (rēbus), 3rd-decl. fīnēs with an agreeing adjective.

image.alt: Imagined portrait of Horace
image.credit: Wikimedia Commons · Anton von Werner

latin: Quidquid id est, timeō Danaōs et dōna ferentēs.
translation: Whatever it is, I fear the Greeks even when they bring gifts.
context: Laocoön, priest of Neptune, warns the Trojans against the wooden horse. Sea serpents sent by the gods kill him soon afterwards.

teaching_value.note: 1st-person present, accusative plurals, present participle (ferentēs), et = "even". (Latin Library prints the old acc. form ferentīs.)

image.alt: Laocoön and his sons, Vatican Museums
image.credit: Wikimedia Commons (CC0) · Wilfredor

latin: Urbem Rōmam ā prīncipiō rēgēs habuēre.
translation: From the beginning, kings ruled the city of Rome.
context: Tacitus opens his history of the emperors with a lightning summary of Rome before them: kings first, then Brutus and the Republic.

teaching_value.note: Object first, subject (rēgēs) last; perfect -ēre = -ērunt. Core words only. Teaches that endings, not word order, carry the meaning.

image.alt: Romulus and Remus with the she-wolf
image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access) · Giulio Romano / Wenceslaus Hollar

latin: Ōrandum est ut sit mēns sāna in corpore sānō.
translation: You should pray for a sound mind in a sound body.
context: Ending a satire on foolish prayers, Juvenal says the only thing worth asking the gods for is a healthy mind in a healthy body.

teaching_value.note: The same adjective agreeing in nom. f. (mēns sāna) and abl. n. (corpore sānō). A perfect agreement drill. Gerundive/subjunctive glossed as a preview.

image.alt: Bronze statuette of Mercury
image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access)

latin: D(īs) M(ānibus) s(acrum). Aur(ēliae) Lupulae mātrī piissimae Dionȳsius Fortūnātus fīlius. S(it) t(ibi) t(erra) l(evis).
translation: Sacred to the spirits of the departed (and) to his very devoted mother Aurelia Lupula: Dionysius Fortunatus, her son, (set this up). May the earth lie lightly on you.
context: A son's tombstone for his mother at Risingham fort, north of Hadrian's Wall. It ends with S·T·T·L, the Roman equivalent of R.I.P., found on epitaphs across the empire.
attribution_note: Text and translation from RIB online (1250). The same formula is spelled out on RIB 693, 1258 and 1405. Stone spelling Lupule/piissime is normalized to -ae.

teaching_value.note: Datives of the person honoured (mātrī piissimae), nominative of the dedicator (fīlius), and the formula abbreviations D·M·S and S·T·T·L. The subjunctive sit is a glossed preview.

image.alt: Roman marble cinerary urn
image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access)

latin: Rōmānae spatium est urbis et orbis idem.
translation: The extent of the Roman city and of the world is the same.
context: At the festival of Terminus, god of boundary stones, Ovid notes that other peoples have fixed borders, but Rome's border is the whole world. Note the play on urbis/orbis.

teaching_value.note: est with a nominative subject and predicate (spatium … idem); the genitives urbis/orbis are a glossed preview. A pun learners remember.

image.alt: Lanciani's map of ancient Rome (Forma Urbis Romae, sheet XV)
image.credit: Rodolfo Lanciani · Rodolfo Lanciani

latin: Atque in perpetuum, frāter, avē atque valē.
translation: And forever, brother, hail and farewell.
context: The last line of Catullus's elegy at his brother's grave near Troy. He came a long way to say goodbye with the old funeral words.

teaching_value.note: Vocative frāter, formulaic imperatives avē/valē (classroom greetings), in + acc. idiom.

image.alt: Marble funerary altar of Cominia Tyche
image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access)

latin: SENATVS POPVLVSQVE ROMANVS DIVO TITO DIVI VESPASIANI F(ILIO) VESPASIANO AVGVSTO — Senātus Populusque Rōmānus Dīvō Titō Dīvī Vespasiānī fīliō Vespasiānō Augustō
translation: The Senate and People of Rome, to the deified Titus Vespasian Augustus, son of the deified Vespasian.
context: Domitian built the arch after his brother Titus died and was deified. Its reliefs show the spoils of the Temple in Jerusalem, captured in AD 70.

source.work: Inscription, Arch of Titus, Rome (CIL VI 945)

attribution_note: Text per Wikipedia "Arch of Titus" (citing CIL VI 945).

teaching_value.note: The full SPQR expanded (-que), dedication in the dative (dīvō Tītō), genitive dīvī Vespasiānī. It turns the familiar SPQR into grammar.

image.alt: Dedicatory inscription on the attic of the Arch of Titus
image.credit: “ArcoTitoIscrizione” by MM, CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0), via Wikimedia Commons; modified: cropped to 2:1, resized

latin: Ōdī et amō. quārē id faciam, fortasse requīris. nesciō, sed fierī sentiō et excrucior.
translation: I hate and I love. Why I do this, perhaps you ask. I don't know, but I feel it happen and I am tormented.
context: Catullus's two-line poem about his love for "Lesbia" has eight verbs and no nouns. It is probably the most compressed love poem in Latin.

teaching_value.note: Verb-heavy: 1st-person present forms, ōdī (perfect form, present meaning), infinitive fierī, passive excrucior. The indirect question (faciam) is just a preview.

image.alt: Roman marble portrait of a young woman
image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access)

latin: Dulce et decōrum est prō patriā morī.
translation: It is sweet and fitting to die for one's country.
context: Horace praises military courage among his "Roman Odes". Wilfred Owen turned the line bitterly against itself in a 1917 poem.

teaching_value.note: Infinitive as the subject (morī) with neuter predicate adjectives; prō + ablative. Good for the Unit 8 infinitive work.

image.alt: Marble head of a helmeted soldier, Flavian period
image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access)

latin: Albānīque patrēs, atque altae moenia Rōmae.
translation: And the Alban fathers, and the walls of lofty Rome.
context: The climax of the Aeneid's opening sentence: Aeneas's wanderings lead to Alba Longa's founding fathers and, finally, to the walls of Rome.

teaching_value.note: Nominative plurals (patrēs, moenia), with -que and atque for "and". The genitive altae … Rōmae is a glossed preview.

image.alt: Surviving stretch of the Servian Wall outside Termini station, Rome
image.credit: Wikimedia Commons · User: (WT-shared) Roundtheworld at wts wikivoyage

latin: Lupus est homō hominī, nōn homō.
translation: Man is a wolf to man, not a man.
context: A merchant refuses to hand money to a stranger: to someone who does not know you, a man is a wolf. The line continues "quom quālis sit nōn nōvit".

teaching_value.note: est linking two nominatives (lupus … homō); the dative hominī is a glossed preview. Fits the Romulus and she-wolf theme.

image.alt: Manuscript page of Plautus, Vatican Pal. lat. 1615
image.credit: Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana · Plautus

latin: Forsan et haec ōlim meminisse iuvābit.
translation: Perhaps one day it will be a pleasure to remember even these things.
context: Shipwrecked on the coast of Africa, Aeneas tries to cheer up his exhausted men with these words.

teaching_value.note: Future iuvābit (1st conj. -bit), impersonal verb with an infinitive, haec as a neut. pl. pronoun. A good Unit 7 future sighting.

image.alt: Sarcophagus with Muses and Sirens (relief strip)
image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access)

latin: Ita fac, mī Lūcīlī: vindicā tē tibi.
translation: Do this, my Lucilius: claim yourself for yourself.
context: The first words of Seneca's first letter to Lucilius. He tells him to take back the time he loses to other people and other things.

teaching_value.note: Two imperatives (fac irregular, vindicā 1st conj.); reflexive tē/tibi shows acc. and dat. of the same pronoun side by side.

image.alt: Roman marble portrait of a man
image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access)

latin: Annōs ūndēvīgintī nātus exercitum prīvātō cōnsiliō et prīvātā impēnsā comparāvī.
translation: At the age of nineteen, on my own initiative and at my own expense, I raised an army.
context: Augustus's own record of his deeds, set up in bronze at his mausoleum. It opens with the private army he raised in 44 BC after Caesar's murder.

teaching_value.note: 1st-person perfect (comparāvī), accusative of extent of time, paired ablatives (prīvātō cōnsiliō, prīvātā impēnsā). A spin-doctored line worth reading critically.

image.alt: Res Gestae text on the Temple of Augustus, Ankara
image.credit: Wikimedia Commons · Unknown authorUnknown author

latin: Prope est ā tē deus, tēcum est, intus est.
translation: God is near you, he is with you, he is within you.
context: Seneca tells Lucilius he need not raise his hands to the sky or ask a temple keeper to let him near a statue's ear. The divine is already within us.

teaching_value.note: est three times; ā + ablative and the joined form tēcum (cum + abl.); deus. Short and nearly all core words.

image.alt: Bronze statuette of Mercury
image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access)

latin: S·P·Q·R — Senātus Populusque Rōmānus
translation: The Senate and the Roman People
context: Four letters stamped on arches, coins, standards and even modern Roman manhole covers. They name the two powers of the Republic, Senate and People.

source.work: Formula on inscriptions, coins and standards

teaching_value.note: Two nominatives, an adjective, and -que. The most-seen Latin abbreviation in the world; ideal for Unit 1.

image.alt: Bronze she-wolf, Capitoline Museums
image.credit: Wikimedia Commons (CC0)

latin: Quot hominēs, tot sententiae.
translation: As many people, so many opinions.
context: An old man asks three legal advisers what to do. Each gives a different answer, and one of them, Hegio, shrugs with this line.

teaching_value.note: No verb at all: two nominative plurals balanced by quot … tot. All core words; a perfect first-week sentence.

image.alt: Ancient comic theatre mask
image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access)

latin: Haec ōrnāmenta sunt mea.
translation: These are my jewels.
context: A wealthy visitor showed off her jewellery. Cornelia kept her talking until her sons came home from school, then pointed to them.

source.work: Valerius Maximus, Facta et Dicta Memorabilia

attribution_note: Text verified in Valerius Maximus, writing ~150 years after Cornelia; the anecdote itself is traditional.

teaching_value.note: Four words: haec (neut. pl.), sunt, possessive mea agreeing with ōrnāmenta. Ideal for the Familia unit.

image.alt: Bartolozzi print: Cornelia presents her sons as her jewels
image.credit: Yale Center for British Art · Francesco Bartolozzi

latin: Fullōnēs ululamque canō, nōn arma virumque.
translation: I sing of fullers and an owl, not of arms and the man.
context: A Pompeian parody of the Aeneid's first line, written on a laundry (fullonica). The fullers' guild had the owl, Minerva's bird, as its emblem.
attribution_note: AGP lists CIL IV 9128 and 9131.

teaching_value.note: Present canō with accusative objects and -que twice. Pairs with the Aeneid "Arma virumque" card (U7) to show real Romans quoting Virgil.

image.alt: Fullonica (laundry) of Stephanus, Pompeii
image.credit: Wikimedia Commons · Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China

latin: Tantaene animīs caelestibus īrae?
translation: Can heavenly minds hold such great anger?
context: Virgil marvels that a goddess, Juno, could nurse such fury against one good man. It sets up the epic's question about divine justice.

teaching_value.note: Dative of possession (animīs caelestibus, "do heavenly minds have…"), 3rd-decl. adjective agreement, -ne question.

image.alt: Statue of Juno Sospita, Vatican Museums
image.credit: Wikimedia Commons · AnonymousUnknown author

latin: Vesta eadem est et terra: subest vigil ignis utrīque.
translation: Vesta and the earth are the same: a wakeful fire lies beneath both.
context: Ovid explains why Vesta's temple in the Forum was round: like the earth, the goddess holds an eternal fire at her centre, tended by the Vestal Virgins.

teaching_value.note: est + predicate, 3rd-decl. ignis with an adjective (vigil), dative with subest.

image.alt: The "Vesta Giustiniani" statue
image.credit: DPLA via Wikimedia Commons · Catsimpoolas, Nicholas; Scull, S. A. (Sarah Amelia)

latin: Dīmidium factī, quī coepit, habet; sapere audē, incipe.
translation: He who has begun has half the deed done; dare to be wise, begin!
context: Horace urges young Lollius not to put off living well, like a fool waiting for a river to finish flowing past before he crosses.

teaching_value.note: Two imperatives (audē, incipe), complementary infinitive (sapere), partitive genitive (dīmidium factī), relative clause with the antecedent left out.

image.alt: Page of Horace's Odes in a 10th-century manuscript, Florence, Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Plut. 34.1
image.credit: Horace, Odes · Biblioteca Medicea Laurenziana, Plut. 34.1

latin: Tū regere imperiō populōs, Rōmāne, mementō … parcere subiectīs et dēbellāre superbōs.
translation: You, Roman, remember to rule the peoples with your power … to spare the conquered and to war down the proud.
context: In the underworld, Anchises shows Aeneas his descendants and defines Rome's mission: leave art and science to the Greeks, and rule.

teaching_value.note: A chain of infinitives after mementō, vocative Rōmāne, dative with parcō. The imperial creed in one sentence.

image.alt: Augustus of Prima Porta
image.credit: Wikimedia Commons · Till Niermann

latin: Arma virumque canō, Trōiae quī prīmus ab ōrīs Ītaliam … vēnit.
translation: I sing of arms and the man who first came from the shores of Troy to Italy.
context: The opening of Rome's national epic. Virgil announces his subject: war, and Aeneas, the Trojan refugee whose descendants founded Rome.

teaching_value.note: Accusative objects joined by -que, a 1st-person verb, ab + ablative, a relative clause. The most quoted opening in Latin.

image.alt: Virgil between two Muses, mosaic, Bardo Museum
image.credit: Bardo Museum, Tunis · Boyd Dwyer

latin: Successus textor amat cōpōnae ancillam nōmine Hiredem, quae quidem illum nōn cūrat.
translation: Successus the weaver loves the innkeeper's slave-girl, named Iris, who does not care for him at all.
context: The start of a Pompeian love-triangle on a wall: a rival answers underneath, mocking Successus. Real people, real handwriting, ordinary Latin.
attribution_note: AGP text: "coponiaes ancilla(m)", "Hiredem (:Iridem)". The spelling here is normalized.

teaching_value.note: S-O-V with 1st-conj. present amat and cūrat, nominative and accusative 1st-decl. nouns. The genitive and relative clause are glossed previews.

image.alt: Pompeian portrait of a couple (Terentius Neo and his wife)
image.credit: Naples Archaeological Museum · Jebulon

latin: Fortīs fortūna adiuvat.
translation: Fortune helps the brave.
context: The clever slave Geta urges young Antipho to face his angry father bravely. The proverb later became the motto of countless regiments.

teaching_value.note: Three words: subject + object + 1st-conj. present. fortīs (= fortēs, acc. pl.) shows word order is free. All core words.

image.alt: Terracotta comic theatre mask
image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access)

latin: M(ārcus) Favōni(us) M(ārcī) f(īlius) Pol(liā tribū) Facilis (centuriō) leg(iōnis) XX; Verēcundus et Novīcius līb(ertī) posuērunt; h(īc) s(itus) e(st).
translation: Marcus Favonius Facilis, son of Marcus, of the Pollian voting-tribe, centurion of the Twentieth Legion, lies buried here; Verecundus and Novicius, his freedmen, set this up.
context: A centurion's tombstone from Colchester, the first Roman capital of Britain. It shows him in full armour, holding his vine-staff. Boudica's rebels may have toppled it in AD 61.
attribution_note: Text and translation from RIB online (200). Boudica connection is a common interpretation of the damage, not certain.

teaching_value.note: A soldier's ID card in Latin: nominative name, rank and legion number with standard abbreviations. The perfect posuērunt and the genitives are glossed previews.

image.alt: Tombstone of the centurion Marcus Favonius Facilis, Colchester
image.credit: “RIB 200” by Udimu, CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0), via Wikimedia Commons; modified: cropped to 2:3, resized

latin: Sed fugit intereā, fugit irreparābile tempus.
translation: But meanwhile it flees, time flees beyond recovery.
context: In a poem on farming, Virgil catches himself lingering over details and reminds himself to move on. This is the source of "tempus fugit".

teaching_value.note: Repeated fugit, 3rd-decl. adjective with a neuter noun. The real source of the motto "tempus fugit". (Latin Library spells it inreparābile.)

image.alt: Ancient Roman sundial, Berlin
image.credit: “Ancient Roman sundial, Antikensammlung Berlin, 141306” by Zde, CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0), via Wikimedia Commons; modified: background removed (cut-out), cropped, resized

latin: Nusquam est quī ubīque est.
translation: The person who is everywhere is nowhere.
context: Seneca warns against skimming many books. A reader who flits everywhere, like a constant traveller, makes acquaintances but never real friends.

teaching_value.note: Antecedent left out before quī (common pattern); est twice; adverb pair nusquam/ubīque.

image.alt: Ancient clay oil lamp
image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access)

latin: Historia vērō testis temporum, lūx vēritātis, vīta memoriae, magistra vītae, nūntia vetustātis …
translation: History is truly the witness of the ages, the light of truth, the life of memory, the teacher of life, the messenger of the past.
context: In Cicero's dialogue on the ideal orator, Antonius argues that only an orator's voice can give history immortality.

teaching_value.note: Five noun + genitive pairs in a row. A perfect genitive drill that mixes 1st and 3rd declension. Contains the famous "magistra vītae".

image.alt: Marble bust of Cicero, Capitoline Museums, Rome, cut out
image.credit: Bust of Cicero, Capitoline Museums, Rome · photo Wilfredo Rafael Rodriguez Hernandez

latin: Mūsa, mihi causās memorā.
translation: Muse, tell me the reasons.
context: Virgil calls on the Muse to explain why Juno, queen of the gods, hounded the dutiful Aeneas through so many disasters.

teaching_value.note: Vocative Mūsa, dative mihi, accusative plural causās, 1st-conj. imperative memorā. Four core words.

image.alt: Marble statue of a seated Muse
image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access)

latin: Facilis dēscēnsus Avernō.
translation: The descent to Avernus is easy.
context: The Sibyl of Cumae warns Aeneas: going down to the underworld is easy, the door of Dis stands open night and day. Coming back up is the real labour.
person: Publius Vergilius Maro (speech of the Sibyl)
attribution_note: Mynors (OCT) prints Avernō; some manuscripts read Avernī.

teaching_value.note: 3rd-decl. adjective facilis with a 4th-decl. noun, the copula left out (est understood), dative of direction (preview).

image.alt: Print of a statue of Pluto, Rijksmuseum
image.credit: Rijksmuseum · Rijksmuseum

latin: Gutta cavat lapidem, cōnsūmitur ānulus ūsū.
translation: A drop hollows out stone; a ring is worn away by use.
context: Writing from exile on the Black Sea, Ovid tells his friend Albinovanus that everything wears down in time, except his own suffering.

teaching_value.note: An active clause and a passive clause side by side; ablative of means (ūsū). Concrete, easy-to-picture vocabulary.

image.alt: Roman glass cup
image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access)

latin: Dīs Mānibus. Flāvīnus, eq(ues) ālae Petr(iānae), signifer, tur(ma) Candidī, an(nōrum) XXV, stīp(endiōrum) VII, h(īc) s(itus) (est).
translation: To the spirits of the departed: Flavinus, trooper of the cavalry regiment Petriana, standard-bearer, from the troop of Candidus, aged 25, of 7 years' service, lies buried here.
context: A 25-year-old standard-bearer rides down a barbarian on his tombstone, now in Hexham Abbey near Hadrian's Wall. Its formula became a pattern for whole careers.
attribution_note: Text and translation from RIB online (1172).

teaching_value.note: Nominative rank titles (eques, signifer) and Roman numerals for age and service. The datives and genitives are glossed previews. The same formula appears on hundreds of stones.

image.alt: Engraving of the tombstone of Flavinus, Hexham (Bruce, 1875)
image.credit: J. Collingwood Bruce, Lapidarium Septentrionale · John Collingwood Bruce

latin: EID·MAR — Īdibus Mārtiīs
translation: On the Ides of March
context: Brutus put this on a silver coin after murdering Caesar: a freedman's cap between two daggers, and the date of the deed. Propaganda you could hold in your hand.

source.work: Coin legend, denarius of Brutus (Crawford, RRC 508/3)

attribution_note: Legend per Wikipedia "Ides of March coin"; RRC 508/3 per CNG catalogue and the Commons file description (obv. BRVT IMP / L PLAET CEST).

teaching_value.note: Ablative of time (Eīdibus, 3rd decl.) with an agreeing adjective; teaches coin abbreviations.

image.alt: Denarius of Brutus: cap of liberty between two daggers, EID MAR
image.credit: “Ides of march coin” by British Museum, CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0), via Wikimedia Commons; modified: background removed (cut-out), cropped, resized

latin: AEGVPTO·CAPTA — Aegyptō captā
translation: Egypt having been captured
context: After defeating Antony and Cleopatra, Octavian struck coins showing a crocodile, symbol of Egypt, now a Roman possession.

source.work: Coin legend, denarius of Octavian (RIC I² 275a)

attribution_note: Legend per Wikipedia "Coins of Augustus"; RIC I² 275a (Italian mint, 28 BC; obv. CAESAR COS VI) per Forum Ancient Coins catalogue and the PAS record SUSS-BA7F45.

gloss.parse: perf. pass. part. abl. sg. f.

teaching_value.note: Ablative absolute of a place name + perfect participle (preview). Short, real, with a vivid image.

image.alt: Denarius of Octavian with crocodile, AEGVPTO CAPTA
image.credit: Wikimedia Commons · Telo

latin: Vīvāmus, mea Lesbia, atque amēmus.
translation: Let us live, my Lesbia, and let us love.
context: Catullus opens his most famous love poem: ignore the gossip of grumpy old men. Suns can set and rise; for us, once our brief light sets, there is one endless night to sleep. So kiss me.

teaching_value.note: Hortatory subjunctive "let us …" (preview), vocative with possessive. Core verbs vīvō and amō.

image.alt: Roman marble portrait of a young woman
image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access)

latin: Expedit esse deōs, et, ut expedit, esse putēmus.
translation: It is useful that there are gods, and, since it is useful, let us believe they exist.
context: In his cheeky handbook on love, Ovid shrugs at piety: believing in gods is convenient, so let us offer incense. A sceptical Roman voice for the Gods unit.

teaching_value.note: Impersonal expedit with accusative + infinitive (preview), hortatory putēmus (preview). Core words, advanced structure.

image.alt: Jupiter of Smyrna, Louvre
image.credit: Wikimedia Commons · Marie-Lan Nguyen

latin: Dum differtur, vīta trānscurrit.
translation: While it is put off, life runs past.
context: Seneca warns Lucilius that if he keeps waiting for tomorrow, his whole life will slip past while he waits.

teaching_value.note: Present passive (differtur) set against an active verb; dum clause. A short preview of the passive.

image.alt: Pompeian memento-mori mosaic: skull, level and wheel
image.credit: Naples Archaeological Museum · Gary Todd from Xinzheng, China

latin: Cēdant arma togae, concēdat laurea laudī.
translation: Let arms yield to the toga, let the laurel give way to praise.
context: Cicero quotes his own verse about his consulship: civilian leadership in the toga should rank above military glory. Critics mocked the line.
attribution_note: Cicero quotes his own lost poem De consulatu suo. Off. 1.77 reads laudī; the better-known variant concēdat laurea linguae is in In Pisonem 72-74 and Quintilian.

teaching_value.note: Dative with cēdō/concēdō (togae, laudī). Jussive subjunctive as a preview; it pairs with the toga/arma vocabulary.

image.alt: Bronze torso of a commander in a cuirass
image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access)

latin: Quō ūsque tandem abūtēre, Catilīna, patientiā nostrā?
translation: How long, Catiline, will you go on abusing our patience?
context: The opening line of Cicero's first speech against Catiline. He launched straight into it in front of the Senate, with the conspirator sitting in the room.

teaching_value.note: Vocative and ablative with ūtor/abūtor; abūtēre is a future deponent (preview). A good partner to the existing Ō tempora card.

image.alt: Bust of Cicero, Glyptothek Munich
image.credit: “Bust of Cicero (GL 325)” by Yair-haklai, CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0), via Wikimedia Commons; modified: background removed (cut-out), cropped, resized

latin: Iacta ālea est.
translation: The die is cast.
context: Crossing the Rubicon in January 49 BC meant civil war. Suetonius reports these words; Plutarch says Caesar spoke a Greek proverb instead.
attribution_note: Manuscripts of Suetonius read iacta alea est; Erasmus emended to iacta alea esto ("let the die be cast"), matching the Greek proverb Plutarch (Pomp. 60, Caes. 32) says Caesar spoke.

gloss.parse: perf. pass. part. nom. sg. f.

teaching_value.note: Three words: perfect passive = participle + est. A sticky anchor for that form in Unit 6.

image.alt: Marble head of Julius Caesar (Tusculum portrait), Museo di Antichità, Turin, cut out
image.credit: Tusculum portrait, Museo di Antichità, Turin · photo Marie-Lan Taÿ Pamart (Jastrow)

latin: Tantae mōlis erat Rōmānam condere gentem!
translation: So great a labour it was to found the Roman people!
context: Virgil sums up seven years of wandering for Aeneas and the Trojans. Founding Rome was a huge, painful effort.

teaching_value.note: Imperfect erat, infinitive as subject, genitive of description (tantae mōlis).

image.alt: Silver denarius of Julius Caesar, 47–46 BC: Aeneas carrying Anchises and the Palladium, inscribed CAESAR
image.credit: Silver denarius of Julius Caesar, 47–46 BCE · The Met, Rogers Fund, 1908 (248033)

latin: … duās tantum rēs ānxius optat, pānem et circēnsēs.
translation: … it anxiously longs for just two things: bread and circuses.
context: Juvenal sneers that the Roman people (populus is the subject of optat), who once handed out commands and legions, now want only free grain and chariot races.

teaching_value.note: Accusative objects (duās rēs, pānem, circēnsēs) with 3rd-decl. nouns. Short, and still used in modern speech.

image.alt: Piranesi etching of the Colosseum
image.credit: Giovanni Battista Piranesi · Giovanni Battista Piranesi

latin: Tantum religiō potuit suādēre malōrum.
translation: So great the evils that religion could prompt.
context: After telling how Agamemnon sacrificed his daughter Iphigenia for a fair wind, the Epicurean poet Lucretius delivers this one-line verdict.

teaching_value.note: possum + complementary infinitive, partitive genitive (tantum … malōrum). A key Epicurean idea for the Philosophers unit.

image.alt: Roman marble bust of Epicurus, Lucretius's master
image.credit: Wikimedia Commons (CC0) · Gary Todd

latin: Tempus edāx rērum, tūque, invidiōsa vetustās, omnia dēstruitis.
translation: Time, devourer of things, and you, envious old age, you destroy everything.
context: In the Metamorphoses' last book, Pythagoras preaches that everything changes. Even Helen weeps in her mirror at her wrinkles.

teaching_value.note: Vocatives addressing abstractions, 2nd-pl. verb with two subjects, objective genitive rērum.

image.alt: Roman marble portrait head of a woman
image.credit: The Metropolitan Museum of Art (Open Access)

latin: Admīror, ō pariēs, tē nōn cecidisse ruīnīs, quī tot scrīptōrum taedia sustineās.
translation: I'm amazed, O wall, that you haven't collapsed in ruins, since you hold up the tedious scribbles of so many writers.
context: A Pompeian wrote this joke couplet, in verse, about graffiti, on a wall already covered in graffiti. Copies were found in at least three places in the town.
attribution_note: AGP text reads "pariens (:paries)"; duplicates EDR158841-2.

teaching_value.note: Vocative ō pariēs is the target. Everything else (an infinitive clause, a subjunctive) is glossed. The point is the joke and the fact that real people wrote it.

image.alt: The Basilica at Pompeii
image.credit: “Basilica, Pompeii 01” by Adam Harangozó, CC BY-SA 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0), via Wikimedia Commons; modified: cropped to 4:3, resized

latin: Vae victīs!
translation: Woe to the conquered!
context: After sacking Rome around 390 BC, the Gallic chief Brennus threw his sword onto the scales as the Romans weighed out their ransom in gold.

source.date: c. 27-9 BC (event 390 BC Varronian; probably 387/386 BC)

attribution_note: Text verified in Livy; words of a Gaul reported ~350 years later.

teaching_value.note: Short but useful: dative plural of a participle used as a noun. A lead-in to the dative in Unit 4.

image.alt: Illustration: Brennus throws his sword on the scales
image.credit: Wikimedia Commons · Paul Lehugeur (1854-1916)

latin: Exēgī monumentum aere perennius.
translation: I have finished a monument more lasting than bronze.
context: Horace closes his three books of Odes by boasting that his poetry will outlast the pyramids. Two thousand years later, he is still right.

teaching_value.note: Perfect exēgī, comparative perennius with an ablative of comparison (aere).

image.alt: Pyramid of Cestius, Rome
image.credit: “Pyramide 564” by Tyrhénienne, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0), via Wikimedia Commons; modified: cropped to 3:4, resized

latin: D(īs) M(ānibus). Rēgīna līberta et coniuge Barātēs Palmyrēnus nātiōne Catuallauna an(nōrum) XXX.
translation: To the spirits of the departed: Regina, his freedwoman and wife, a Catuvellaunian by tribe, aged 30. Barates of Palmyra (set this up).
context: A Syrian trader from Palmyra freed and married Regina, a British woman. He set up her tombstone at South Shields. Below the Latin he added a line in his own Palmyrene Aramaic.
attribution_note: Text and translation from RIB online (1065). coniuge for coniunx is the stonecutter's.

teaching_value.note: Family words in the nominative (Rēgīna, līberta) and abbreviations (D M, AN). The case of coniuge is non-standard (it stands for coniūnx), so the grammar beyond nominatives is preview only.

image.alt: Tombstone of Regina, South Shields, with Latin and Palmyrene text
image.credit: “Reginas-Tombstone-a-relief-portrait-with-inscriptions-in-Latin-and-Palmyrene-Copyright” by Abigail Baker and Alison Cooley, CC BY 4.0 (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0), via Wikimedia Commons; modified: cropped to 2:3, resized
